title: Unit Circle Definition
text: $$\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$$ represents the y-coordinate of the point on the unit circle at the angle $$\frac{\pi}{4}.$$\n##figure4.gif##

figureAlts.figure4.gif: Diagram of the coordinate (cosine of pi over 4, sine of pi over 4) on the unit circle. The point is located one-eighth of the way around the circumference of the entire circle in the first quadrant. The angle between the positive horizontal axis and the line from the origin to the point going counterclockwise is pi over 4 radians.

title: Reference Angle
text: The reference angle for $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ is $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ itself. The absolute values of the coordinates are given by the legs of a $$45-45-90$$ triangle with hypotenuse $$1$$. The $$x-$$ coordinate and $$y-$$ coordinate lengths are equal and satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: $$1=\sqrt{x**2+x**2}=\sqrt{2}x,$$ so both coordinates are $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$\n##figure5.gif##

figureAlts.figure5.gif: Right triangle: two 45° angles, hypotenuse 1, both legs 1 over square root of 2

title: Quadrant Sign
text: The angle $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ is in the first quadrant, where y-coordinates are positive. Therefore, $$\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$\n##figure6.gif##

figureAlts.figure6.gif: Diagram of the coordinate (cosine of pi over 4, sine of pi over 4) on the unit circle. The point is located one-eighth of the way around the circumference of the entire circle in the first quadrant. The angle between the positive horizontal axis and the line from the origin to the point going counterclockwise is pi over 4 radians.
